query: For lightweight high-entropy alloys intended for weight-critical aerospace and rail-transport applications, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain their ability—or inability—to combine low density with mechanical strength, corrosion resistance, and high-temperature oxidation resistance? Specify an unnamed controlled comparison that would test the hypothesis, the observations predicted relative to a baseline alloy, the conditions under which the hypothesis should cease to hold, the existing observations that support it, and a result that would falsify it.

In many applications, HEAs can significantly outperform traditional and super-alloys, especially at low and high temperatures,. Recently, the design of lightweight HEAs (with a density lower than 5 g/cc) has become one of the hottest research topics in metallurgy. The design of traditional alloys typically relies on one or two primary elements, with the minor addition of other elements to regulate properties such as strength, ductility, corrosion resistance and so on, such as steel, aluminium alloys and titanium alloys. This single-primary-element design approach inevitably imposes limitations on alloy composition design. In view of this, Yeh proposed the concept of high-entropy alloys (HEAs) in 2004 [], which were denoted as multi-principal elements alloys composed of five or more elements, with each element’s content ranging from 5 at.% to 35 at.%. HEAs concept significantly expands the compositional space for alloy design and provides new ideas for the development of novel alloy materials. Compared to traditional alloys, HEAs exhibit a range of exceptional properties, such as outstanding corrosion resistance, remarkable high-temperature strength, and good low-temperature plasticity [,,,,]. These characteristics suggest significant potential for application in fields such as aerospace and marine structures. High-entropy alloys (HEAs), a novel class of multi-principal element alloys, brought a new era in the study of alloy materials []. The presence of five or more elements in close proximity to the iso-atomic ratio endows alloys with high configurational entropy, which confers upon HEAs the capacity to form stable simple solid solution phases. This, in turn, endows HEAs with exceptional mechanical properties and commendable corrosion resistance []. This property gives high-entropy alloys excellent mechanical and physical properties, including high strength, high fracture toughness, and the ability to conduct electricity at very low temperatures []. In addition, they exhibit excellent resistance to high-temperature oxidation and corrosion. Consequently, in the aerospace field [], where the temperature of service varies widely, in the field of ultra-high temperature structural materials [], in marine industrial equipment [], and in the nuclear industry [], where there are harsh working conditions, high-entropy alloys have a wider range of application prospects than traditional alloys due to their rich elemental composition and flexible selection of elemental content.
